edges.effect_quant: Across older-adult studies, tricyclic antidepressants are repeatedly linked to worse cognitive performance or higher risk of later cognitive impairment, largely through anticholinergic burden. In the Women's Health Initiative Memory Study, tricyclic use was associated with incident mild cognitive impairment with HR 1.78 (95% CI 0.99 to 3.21). A meta-analysis of anticholinergic drugs in adults aged 65 and older found class exposure associated with 45% higher odds of cognitive impairment, and a German primary-care cohort found more potentially inappropriate medication exposure, with amitriptyline among the common PRISCUS drugs, associated with reduced cognitive test performance.
edges.population: older adults exposed to tricyclic antidepressants, especially amitriptyline-class drugs in multimorbid or cognitively vulnerable populations
edges.mechanism: Tricyclic antidepressants can impair cognition through strong central antimuscarinic effects that interfere with attention, working memory, and encoding. Sedation, orthostasis, and cumulative anticholinergic burden may further worsen executive function and lower cognitive reserve in older adults.
edges.summary: The most defensible reading is that tricyclic antidepressants are cognitively unfriendly in older adults, even if the exact long-term effect size varies. Direct late-life data and broader anticholinergic literature both point in the same direction, which is why geriatric prescribing frameworks consistently push TCAs down the preference list when cognition matters.
edges.caveats: Not every study isolates TCAs cleanly from depression severity or other anticholinergic drugs, so some of the long-term association could reflect confounding by indication or overall medication burden. Even so, the short-term pharmacologic plausibility and the repeated observational signal make a harmful interpretation more credible than a neutral one.
